title: Slab guard rails and eviction fencepost playbook for KV cache memory amplification
creator: Asha Patel
description: Summary: A regional capacity incident on 2025-02-16 revealed progressive memory amplification in the KV cache leading to OOM-driven evictions and cascading latency spikes. Root cause analysis indicates a fencepost bug in the eviction scoring path combined with an async slab compaction race that allowed ghost prefetched entries to persist without proper reference accounting. The bug surfaced under bursty prefix distribution and was amplified by an experimental prefetch heuristic. Immediate mitigation (rollback and throttles) restored capacity, but the incident requires a coordinated follow-up to avoid recurrence.
impact_timeline: 2025-02-16 03:12 UTC - first alerts from autoscaling; 03:25 UTC - error budget breaches for two services; 03:40 UTC - rollback of prefetch heuristic deployed (PR #5587); 04:05 UTC - temporary eviction backpressure enabled; 06:00 UTC - incident declared resolved after steady memory profile; postmortem began 2025-02-17.
root_cause: Eviction score underflow for certain prefix families due to integer truncation and fencepost iteration bounds in eviction_score.c combined with concurrent async compaction that could detach slab metadata without decrementing reference counts. Experimental prefetch added entries that bypassed normal lifecycle, creating ghost entries that prevented slabs from being reclaimed and amplified memory usage during capacity spikes.
short_term_actions: 1) Roll back prefetch heuristic (done 2025-02-16). 2) Add emergency eviction backpressure flag 'evict_backpressure=on' to runtime config and enable for affected clusters (done). 3) Patch immediate fencepost guard: add bounds checks and safe-early-exit in eviction_score loop (hotfix applied and smoke-tested). 4) Add alerting for slab non-reclamation rate and sudden refcount deltas. 5) Schedule canary rollout of hotfix to dedicated regions with extended heap and telemetry capture.
long_term_actions: 1) Rework eviction scoring to use 64-bit counters and deterministic hysteresis logic to avoid oscillation. 2) Introduce deterministic slab compaction ordering and ensure compaction holds references until the writepath completes. 3) Add checksum/epoch metadata on slab headers to detect ghost entries and force-safe-sweep on mismatch. 4) Harden prefetch: require explicit TTL and lifecycle registration; gate behind feature flag with load-shedding. 5) Expand unit/integration tests: concurrent compaction + eviction chaos test harness; fuzz eviction score boundary conditions. 6) Delivery plan targets runtime-1.19.2.
acceptance_criteria: 1) No slab non-reclamation alerts in 48h under simulated burst workload. 2) Eviction score histograms show hysteresis and no negative/underflow bins. 3) Prefetch feature disabled by default and gated by flag. 4) Canary nodes sustain 1 week of normal traffic without memory trend growth > 5%/24h. 5) Telemetry dashboards + runbook updated and triaged.
rollback_plan: If canary memory trends exceed thresholds or client-facing latency regresses, immediately flip 'evict_backpressure' to off and revert the hotfix via automated canary rollback. Keep prefetch feature disabled until gated releases are validated. Communicate rollback on #incidents and update paging rota.
telemetry_changes: New metrics to emit: slab_reclaimed_count, slab_gc_duration_ms, eviction_score_distribution, refcount_delta_rate, ghost_entry_detected{yes|no}. Dashboards: kvcache/mod_reclaim and kvcache/eviction_hysteresis. Alerts: slab_reclaim_rate < baseline*0.5 for 10m and refcount_delta_rate spike > 1000/min.
qa_and_testing: Create integration harness that replays production prefix distributions (dataset: kvcache-replay-2025-02-01), run concurrent compaction + evict fuzzers for 72h in CI resource pool. Add regression test to performance suite ensuring no >10% mem increase after 100k mixed ops.

notes: Tradeoffs discussed: full refcounting semantics add CPU overhead (~2-3%) but provide strong safety; alternative lightweight epoch checks are cheaper but less robust. We chose refcount+epoch for initial hardening and will iterate if CPU impact is unacceptable.
